extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians, and researchers interested in the nature of mathematical explanation (graduate students and scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether and to what extent a mathematical proof explains (gives the 'why' rather than merely the 'that') using philosophical accounts (Steiner, Lange, Kitcher, counterfactual, internalist). Produce scores or judgments along multiple dimensions such as characterizing properties, unification, counterfactual dependence, and cognitive understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of the reasoned fact (διότι) vs. proof of the fact (ὅτι)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish proofs that merely establish that a conclusion is true (ὅτι, 'that') from proofs that establish why the conclusion holds (διότι, 'why').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the core distinction: a 'good proof' rubric must separately measure explanatoriness (why) in addition to correctness (that). A judgment should ask: does this proof tell us why the theorem holds or only verify its truth?

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizing property used (Steiner)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is explanatory when it deduces the conclusion from a characterizing property — a property unique to the entity in question within its domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests: (1) Vary the characterizing property: does the proof yield a corresponding theorem under deformation? If so, the original was explanatory; if not, it was an accidental verification. (2) Reverse test: change the conclusion; does the proof break in a corresponding way? Anti-example: use of generic machinery (e.g., a generating-function trick) that does not invoke what is specific to the object counts as non-explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry exploited (Lange)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof of a symmetric result is explanatory if it derives that symmetry from a corresponding symmetry in the setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the proof shows how the symmetry of the conclusion follows from some symmetry in definitions, hypotheses, or structure. If the proof treats the result as accidental and does not connect to the underlying symmetry, it scores lower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity exploited (Lange)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof of a simple result is explanatory if it exploits a similar simplicity in the setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the proof's simplicity mirrors or arises from a simple feature of the premises or set-up, rather than obscuring it via complicated or roundabout methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modal/necessity constraint shown (Lange)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof of a mathematically necessary truth is explanatory if it shows the constraint that forces the necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the proof makes manifest why the truth is necessary (what structural constraint prevents variation) rather than merely establishing the necessity by derivation alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument-pattern frugality (Kitcher)
rubrics_metrics.description: How many distinct derivation patterns does the explanation use? Fewer patterns (more frugal) increase explanatoriness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count and classify argument-patterns used by the proof; proofs that instantiate a small set of patterns that apply to many results are more explanatory than proofs relying on many idiosyncratic patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stringency of patterns (Kitcher)
rubrics_metrics.description: How restrictive is each derivational pattern? More restrictive (tighter) patterns are more explanatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the patterns used are highly constrained so that they rule out many alternatives; highly stringent patterns contribute to unificatory power and thus higher explanatoriness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion coverage / unification breadth (Kitcher)
rubrics_metrics.description: How many results follow from the same pattern? Greater coverage (many conclusions explained by the pattern) indicates stronger explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how widely the proof's argument-patterns apply: proofs that show a single pattern accounting for many theorems are favored over isolated one-off tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfactual relevance (CF1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If explanatory fact F were false, would the explanandum G be false? (Relevance condition.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test counterfactual dependence: determine whether the proposed explanatory fact is such that its absence would render the explained fact false. This requires reasoning about changes to mathematical structure (considering 'impossible' or varied setups) to operationalize relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfactual asymmetry (CF2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Asymmetry: it must not be the case that if G were false, F would be false (i.e., explanation relation should be asymmetric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the asymmetry condition to ensure the proposed explanatory relation isn't symmetric; this distinguishes genuine explanations from mere correlations or mutual dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generates understanding in trained readers (Internalist / Inglis & Mejía-Ramos)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is explanatory to the extent it generates understanding in suitably trained readers by cognitive mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize via three markers: (1) directs attention to conceptually significant sections, (2) reorganizes information into coherent schemas, (3) reduces cognitive load on working memory. This account invites empirical testing: explanatoriness = what produces understanding in trained readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-relative constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatoriness is proof-relative (a theorem may have explanatory and non-explanatory proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, treat explanatoriness as a property of the particular proof under consideration rather than of the theorem alone; compare different proofs of the same theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-relative constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatoriness is partially audience-relative — what explains for one audience (e.g., undergraduates) may not explain for another (e.g., researchers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify the intended audience or expertise level when judging explanatoriness; a proof may score differently for different reader groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-relative constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatoriness is partially context-relative — what counts as explanatory depends on what was previously puzzling and the surrounding mathematical context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the prior knowledge, background expectations, and the specific question that prompted the explanation; a proof answering a specific puzzle is more explanatory in that context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: use of generic machinery without invoking specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that use generic machinery that does not invoke what is specific to the object score low on explanatoriness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag proofs that achieve the result via 'black-box' tools or standard tricks without connecting the argument to the characterizing features of the object; these are often 'accidental verifications' per Steiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: 'magic trick' proofs (unanticipated manipulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that establish the conclusion through a manipulation no one could have anticipated (a 'magic trick') are low on explanatoriness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such proofs may verify truth but fail to reveal underlying structure or reasons; they are judged non-explanatory despite correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: verification without revealing structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Long or mechanical verifications (e.g., lengthy induction) that do not present an organizing idea score low on explanatoriness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for absence of an organizing concept or schema; if the proof merely checks cases or runs computations without structural insight, penalize explanatoriness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: hiding asymmetries
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that 'hide asymmetries' — work equally well for related true and false claims — indicate lack of explanatory asymmetry and score low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the method treats distinctions that matter to the result; if the method would also prove nearby false statements, it fails counterfactual/asymmetry tests.
